title: The impact of household connection to public network wastewater systems: Regulatory impact assessment
rationale: Excluded (E12: Wrong study design). This 2019 paper conducts an ex-ante Regulatory Impact Assessment (RIA) using Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (M-MACBETH) and prospective cost-benefit projections (modeled over 2016-2023 / 2017-2026) to help the Minas Gerais regulator (ARSAE) rank four hypothetical wastewater diffusion targets (100%, 75%, 50%, and 0% reductions in non-connected households). Household connection levels are assumed ex ante as scenario definitions rather than empirically observed outcomes, and primary data collection is restricted to stakeholder elicitation of subjective value functions and criteria weights. In addition, while the paper satisfies the plain reading of Criterion 2 by examining RIA as a regulatory governance tool, it fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading because the evaluated alternatives are generic infrastructure-diffusion targets rather than legal or administrative rules governing household access; because it lacks an empirical evaluation design measuring observed access outcomes, plain_criterion2_decision is also exclude.

title: "The organised encroachment of the powerful"-Everyday practices of public space and water supply in Dhaka, Bangladesh
rationale: This qualitative socio-legal empirical study (2008–2010) examines household drinking-water access in an informal settlement (bosti) of Dhaka, Bangladesh. It meets all inclusion criteria, including the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2, because it empirically analyses how statutory tenure rules excluding settlements on public land from direct DWASA connections, the 2007 DWASA rule change permitting supply via slum committees regardless of tenure, selective DWASA inspection enforcement/bribery, and landlord-tenant contractual mediation shape household water connections, quantity, continuity, exclusion, and affordability. Qualitative empirical studies are eligible for systematic-review mechanism synthesis even without a quantitative effect size.

rationale: Full text matches metadata (Hove et al. 2019, BMJ Global Health). title: Stealing from the poor? Game theory and the politics of water markets in Chile
rationale: Exclude under E07 (Wrong service; see Exclusion Criterion 7: 'Water-resource studies unrelated to household or community service access'). Galaz (2004) uses game theory, 11 secondary conflict cases, and 9 key-informant interviews to examine why powerful actors (industrial farmers, mining companies, aquaculture firms, real estate investors, and bulk raw-water extractors) violate the raw surface/groundwater and agricultural irrigation rights of peasant farmers (campesinos) and rural indigenous communities under Chile's 1981 Water Code. Even when an urban water utility (SENDOS/ESSAT) appears in one case and in the game model, it is analysed as a bulk raw-water extractor competing with downstream agricultural irrigators, not in relation to household or community drinking-water or sanitation service delivery, connection, tariffs, or domestic access. Both under the narrow 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 reading and the plain Criterion 2 wording, the study is excluded because it fails Criterion 1 (service access) and Criterion 4 (service access outcome).

title: Bridging political economy analysis and critical institutionalism: An approach to help analyse institutional change for rural water services
rationale: This qualitative multi-level case study (2010-2011 fieldwork in Mali) satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings of Criterion 2. Beyond its theoretical synthesis of political economy analysis and critical institutionalism, it empirically examines rule-type mechanisms directly governing sustained rural drinking water access—specifically national user cost-recovery rules, municipal-community O&M cost-sharing rules, case-by-case discretionary accommodation of user breakdown contributions based on community ability to pay, formal accounting requirements to access municipal co-funding, and locally adapted household water tariff schedules across 8 case study villages. It links local cost-sharing and repair co-funding to rural water service availability/reliability (90% handpump functionality in the focal municipality vs 71% across rural Mali) and documents affordability/revenue limits under national full cost-recovery rules. Confidence is set to medium because Footnote 1 notes that fuller empirical data and results from the same research are reported in companion articles (Jones 2013a, b), leaving methodological and village-level access outcome reporting relatively concise here.

rationale: Excluded as E03 (Wrong exposure) under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification. title: The impact of neo-liberalism on water and sanitation provision in the informal settlements: Towards the re-enforcement of gendered roles or democratic emancipation?
rationale: Full-text qualitative comparative case study (participant observation and 15 in-depth interviews across Banana City in Durban and Endlovini in Cape Town) examining women's household and community access to water and sanitation in informal settlements. Although the overarching 'neo-liberalism' (GEAR) framing is macro-governance background (communal standpipe water is provided free without restriction under municipal Free Basic Water / Indigent policies in both settlements), the primary empirical findings directly examine rule-type legal and administrative mechanisms governing service access under Criterion 2: temporary-shelter administrative status creating uncertainty over upgrading/infrastructure qualification, landowner-consent rules blocking municipal water/sanitation installation on non-municipal land, a 5-month water disconnection in Banana City resolved through anti-eviction litigation and municipal agreement to purchase and legalize the land, limits of Free Basic Water / Indigent policies without legal tenure and reticulation infrastructure, and municipal locking of communal toilets in Endlovini. Satisfies all review inclusion criteria (c1–c6) for qualitative mechanism synthesis.
